title: Email Marketing for Divorce Lawyers: A Practical Guide | CaseAuthority
meta: Email marketing for divorce lawyers: who to email, follow-up after consultations, safe and discreet emails, referral newsletters, the rules and what to measure.
h1: Email Marketing for Divorce Lawyers: Stay in Touch Without Overstepping
lead: Very few people hire a divorce lawyer the first time they think about divorce. Many spend weeks or months reading, worrying and talking to friends before they book a consultation, and many book one and then go quiet while they decide. Email is one of the few ways to stay helpful during that long, private decision without being pushy. This guide is for divorce and family law attorneys who want to use email well: who to email and who not to, what to send after a consultation, how to keep emails safe and discreet when a spouse might see them, how to stay in touch with past clients and referral partners, the rules that apply, and how to tell whether email is bringing retained clients.
quick_answer: Email marketing for divorce lawyers means sending useful, discreet emails to people who have asked to hear from your firm, such as people who booked or requested a consultation, downloaded a guide, became clients in the past, or refer clients to you, like therapists and financial advisors. It works because divorce decisions take time, and email keeps your firm in mind while people get ready. The best family law emails are helpful rather than salesy, use safe subject lines and sender names, go only to addresses the person chose, include a clear way to unsubscribe and your postal address, follow your state bar rules, and are judged by consultations and retainers, not opens.
takeaways: Many people research for months. Email keeps you helpful and remembered while they decide.
Consultation requests, guide downloads, past clients and referral partners, not bought lists.
Use the address the person chose, discreet subject lines and no case details in marketing emails.
A short, kind sequence after a consultation often brings back people who went quiet.
Therapists, financial planners and other lawyers send cases to firms they remember.
Track booked consultations and retainers that came from email.

sections.h2: Why Does Email Marketing Work for Divorce and Family Law Firms?
sections.answer: Because most divorce clients take a long time to decide, and email lets your firm stay helpful and familiar during that time without paying for every contact.
paras: A car accident victim may hire a lawyer within days. Divorce is different. People often start quietly searching for answers long before they are ready to file. They want to know what happens to the house, how custody works, what a divorce might cost and whether they should talk to a lawyer before they talk to their spouse. Many book a consultation and then wait.

That long, private decision is where email shines. Someone who downloaded your guide to preparing for divorce, or who met with you and said they needed time, can hear from your firm every few weeks with something genuinely useful. When they are ready, your name is the one they already trust.

Email is also something you own. Ads stop when you stop paying, and social media reach goes up and down. Your list of people who asked to hear from you stays with your firm. Family law email marketing works best alongside the channels that bring people to you in the first place, which we cover in our guide to [[a:family-law-marketing|family law marketing]].

sections.h2: Who Should a Divorce Lawyer Email?
sections.answer: People who have asked to hear from your firm: consultation requests, people who downloaded a guide or signed up on your website, past clients who agreed to stay in touch, and referral partners.
paras: The safest and most useful lists are built from people who gave you their email for a reason. Each group needs different emails, so keep them separate from the start.
list: People who requested or booked a consultation but have not hired you yet
People who downloaded a checklist or guide from your website, such as a divorce preparation checklist
People who signed up for updates or a newsletter on your site
Past clients who agreed to hear from you after their case closed
Referral partners, such as therapists, financial advisors, mediators, accountants and other lawyers

sections.h2: Who Should a Divorce Lawyer Not Email?
sections.answer: Bought lists, people who never asked to hear from you, the other party in a case, and any address you are not sure belongs only to the person you mean to reach.
paras: Buying email lists is a bad idea for any law firm and a worse one in family law. People did not ask to hear from you, many addresses are out of date, and sending to them can damage your email reputation and break the rules covered later in this guide.

Be especially careful with the other side of a case. Never add an opposing party to a marketing list, even by accident, for example because they once filled in a form on your website. Your intake system should mark opposing parties and conflicts so they are never emailed.

Also think about shared email accounts. Couples often share a family email address or a laptop. If someone contacts you from an address their spouse can read, sending regular emails about divorce could put them in a very difficult or even unsafe position. Always ask which address is safe to use and respect the answer.

sections.h2: How Do You Keep Divorce Emails Safe and Discreet?
sections.answer: Ask for a safe address, use neutral sender names and subject lines, keep case details out of marketing emails, and make it easy to stop emails at any time.
paras: Privacy and safety should shape every part of email marketing in family law. Some people are leaving a controlling or abusive relationship, and an email arriving at the wrong moment can make things worse. A little care goes a long way.

At intake and on every signup form, ask the person which email address is safe to use and whether it is fine for your firm to send helpful emails. Use a sender name that is your firm's name or the attorney's name, not something like Divorce Help. Write subject lines that would not raise questions if someone glanced at a screen, such as Your checklist from our office, rather than Ready to file for divorce?

Keep anything about a specific case out of marketing emails. Updates about a client's matter belong in your secure client communication, not in a newsletter tool. If someone mentions they feel unsafe, have intake share emergency resources such as the National Domestic Violence Hotline and pause all marketing emails to them.

sections.h2: What Should You Send After a Divorce Consultation?
sections.answer: A short, helpful follow-up sequence: a thank-you with a summary of next steps, a few useful resources over the next weeks, and an easy way to come back when they are ready.
paras: Many people leave a consultation feeling overwhelmed. They may need to talk to family, look at their finances or simply wait for the right time. A gentle follow-up sequence keeps the door open without pressure.

A simple sequence might start with a thank-you email the same day that sums up the general next steps you discussed and how to book again. A week or two later, send something useful, such as a checklist of documents to gather. After that, send an occasional email with answers to common questions, such as how custody schedules usually work or what happens to retirement accounts. Each email should end with one clear, low-pressure invitation to call or book.
Keep these emails general. Do not repeat personal details from the consultation, because emails can be forwarded or seen by others. Stop the sequence as soon as someone hires you or asks you to stop.

sections.h2: What Topics Work Best in Family Law Emails?
sections.answer: Clear answers to the questions people are afraid to ask, practical checklists, and short explanations of how the process works in your state.
paras: The best family law emails feel like a calm, knowledgeable friend. They explain, they reassure and they help people take the next small step. They do not pressure, frighten or make promises.
list: How to prepare for a divorce consultation and what to bring
What happens to the house, retirement accounts and debts, in general terms
How custody and parenting time decisions are usually made
Mediation, collaborative divorce and going to court, and how they differ
How long a divorce usually takes in your state and what slows it down
Talking to children about divorce, with links to trusted resources
After the divorce: updating wills, beneficiaries and accounts, and when orders can be changed

sections.h2: Should Divorce Lawyers Send a Newsletter to Past Clients?
sections.answer: Often yes, if past clients agreed to it. Past family law clients come back for modifications and refer friends, and a light, useful newsletter keeps your firm in mind.
paras: A divorce rarely ends every legal need. Parenting plans change as children grow, people move, incomes change and support orders may need review. Past clients may also need help with a prenuptial agreement before remarrying, or an estate plan after the divorce. And many people going through a divorce ask a friend who has been through one for a lawyer's name.

A newsletter every month or two can cover changes in the law, reminders to update beneficiaries and wills, and short guides on modifications. Keep it warm and brief. Many former clients will not want frequent reminders of a hard time in their lives, so make the unsubscribe link easy to find and never take it personally.
Ask before adding anyone. A simple question when a case closes, such as whether they would like to receive occasional updates, respects their choice and keeps your list clean.

sections.h2: How Can Email Help Divorce Lawyers Get More Referrals?
sections.answer: By keeping your firm in front of the professionals who meet people before they hire a lawyer, such as therapists, financial advisors, mediators and other attorneys.
paras: Many family law cases come from referrals. Marriage and family therapists, financial planners who work with divorcing clients, accountants, mediators and lawyers in other practice areas all meet people who need a divorce lawyer. They refer to the firms they know and remember.

A short, professional email for referral partners every month or two can share updates that matter to their work, such as changes in how your state treats retirement accounts in divorce, a new attorney joining the firm, or a guide they can give their clients. It keeps the relationship alive between coffees and calls.

Be careful with how referral relationships work. Most states do not let lawyers pay or give anything of value for a recommendation, apart from limited exceptions, so referral emails should share useful information, not rewards. Our guide to [[a:blog/family-law-marketing-ideas|family law marketing ideas]] covers more ways to build referral relationships.

sections.h2: What Rules Apply to Email Marketing for Law Firms?
sections.answer: Federal email law, your state bar's lawyer advertising rules and the rules of the major email providers all apply, along with your duty to protect client confidences.
paras: In the United States, the CAN-SPAM Act sets basic rules for commercial email. Messages must include a working way to opt out and a valid physical postal address, and opt-out requests must be honored within 10 business days. Subject lines and sender names must not be misleading.

Marketing emails are also lawyer advertising. They must be truthful and not misleading, must not promise results, and must follow your state's rules on things like case results, testimonials and specialist claims. Some states require certain labels on advertising sent to people who are not current clients. Rules on direct contact with prospective clients vary, so check how your state treats email to people who did not ask to hear from you.

Confidentiality matters too. Do not put anything in a marketing email that reveals someone is or was a client, or details about their matter, unless they have clearly agreed. Use separate email tools and lists for client communication and for marketing. This guide is general information, not legal or ethics advice, so check your own state's rules.

sections.h2: How Do You Make Sure Your Emails Reach the Inbox?
sections.answer: Send from your own domain, set up the email authentication records providers expect, send only to people who asked, and keep spam complaints low.
paras: Email providers decide whether your message lands in the inbox, the promotions tab or the spam folder. Google's sender guidelines, for example, ask senders to set up email authentication such as SPF or DKIM, keep spam complaint rates low, and offer an easy unsubscribe. Larger senders have extra requirements.

In practice, this means sending from an address at your firm's own domain, not a free email account, and asking whoever manages your domain to set up the authentication records your email tool provides. Use a reputable email marketing or legal CRM tool, rather than sending large batches from your normal inbox.
List quality matters more than size. A small list of people who asked to hear from you will reach more inboxes, and bring more consultations, than a large list of people who did not.

sections.h2: How Often Should a Family Law Firm Send Emails?
sections.answer: Often enough to stay remembered and rarely enough to stay welcome: a few emails in the weeks after a consultation, then every few weeks to a couple of months depending on the list.
paras: There is no perfect number, and each list is different. Someone who just met with you may welcome a few helpful emails over the next month. Past clients usually prefer much less, perhaps every couple of months. Referral partners are busy professionals and appreciate short, occasional updates.

Watch the signals. If unsubscribes or complaints rise after a change, slow down or make the emails more useful. If people reply with questions, you are probably getting it right. Consistency matters more than volume: a short, useful email every few weeks beats a burst of emails followed by silence.

sections.h2: How Do You Measure Email Marketing for a Divorce Practice?
sections.answer: Track the consultations booked and retainers signed from email, along with replies, clicks and unsubscribes, rather than relying on open rates.
paras: Open rates used to be the main email number, but they are less reliable now because some email apps load messages automatically, which can count as an open even if nobody read it. Clicks, replies and booked consultations tell you much more.

Give each email a clear next step, such as booking a consultation or reading a guide, and track it with links that show the email as the source. Ask every new client how they found you, and if they mention an email or a guide they downloaded, record that in your intake or case management system.

Over a few months, you can see how many consultations and retainers came from people on your lists, which emails led to them, and which groups of people respond best. That shows you where to spend your time.

sections.h2: Common Email Mistakes Divorce Lawyers Make
sections.answer: Buying lists, emailing shared or unsafe addresses, salesy subject lines, putting case details in marketing emails, and only measuring opens.
paras: Other mistakes include sending the same email to every group, forgetting the unsubscribe link or postal address, making promises about outcomes, and stopping after one or two emails because nobody hired right away. Divorce decisions take time, and a patient, steady approach usually wins.
list: Ask for a safe email address and permission at intake
Keep separate lists for prospects, past clients and referral partners
Use neutral sender names and subject lines
Never include case details in marketing emails
Include an unsubscribe link and your postal address in every email
Measure consultations and retainers, not just opens

sections.answer: This article is general information about marketing, not legal or ethics advice.
paras: Email results depend on your market, your lists, your practice areas, your website, your intake and the work done. Nothing here is a promise of any result.

Rules on lawyer advertising, client confidentiality, commercial email and contacting prospective clients vary by state and change over time. Check your state bar's rules before launching or changing any email marketing.

faq.q: Does Email Marketing Work for Divorce Lawyers?
faq.a: It can work well because divorce decisions often take weeks or months. Helpful, discreet emails to people who asked to hear from you keep your firm in mind until they are ready to hire. Results depend on list quality, useful content and fast follow-up when someone replies.

faq.q: What Should a Divorce Lawyer Put in a Newsletter?
faq.a: Short, useful updates such as changes in family law, reminders to update wills and beneficiaries after divorce, guides on custody or support modifications, and answers to common questions. Avoid case details and anything that reads like a hard sell.

faq.q: Is It Legal for Lawyers to Send Marketing Emails?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the emails follow federal email rules such as the CAN-SPAM Act and your state bar's lawyer advertising rules. That generally means a working unsubscribe link, your postal address, honest subject lines and no misleading claims. Some states have extra labeling rules.

faq.q: How Do I Build an Email List for My Family Law Firm?
faq.a: Offer something genuinely useful on your website, such as a divorce preparation checklist, ask consultation requests for permission to send helpful emails, and invite past clients and referral partners to opt in. Never buy lists.

faq.q: How Often Should I Email Prospective Divorce Clients?
faq.a: A few helpful emails in the weeks after a consultation request, then every few weeks, usually works well. Slow down if unsubscribes rise and stop immediately if someone asks or hires you.

faq.q: Can a Spouse See Emails From My Firm?
faq.a: If the person uses a shared email account or device, yes. That is why you should always ask which address is safe, use discreet sender names and subject lines, and keep case details out of marketing emails.
